newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: El Al ponders Schiphol move after cargo plane ban.
newsitem.headline: El Al ponders Schiphol move after cargo plane ban.

text.p: El Al, one of Amsterdam Airport Schiphol's top freight carriers, may be forced to consider moving its freight hub following the Dutch airport's move to ban some aircraft taking-off during the night.

Schiphol announced Friday that in order to keep down noise levels, the aircraft in question -- the DC-10, Boeing 747-100, 747-200, 747-300 and the 747SP -- will not be able to take off from the airport between 1100 hours and 0600 hours from August 1.

Israel Chervin, cargo manager of the Israel carrier El Al, said: "At the moment we are very surprised concerning this ban and are not sure what we will do. El Al has been calling at this airport for around 40 years.
"The take-off ban details have been sent to the airline's Tel Aviv headquarters and we are awaiting a reaction," he added.
El Al operates around 20 movements a week, representing around 2,000 cargo tonnes, into Schiphol with 747-100 and 747-200 freighters.
Chervin estimated that six or seven of these flights take off during the soon-to-be-banned period.
He added that it would be impossible to change many of the schedules because they were largely dictated by the perishable industry in Israel.
Flowers were picked and processed during the day in Israel and the flights left at around 8 pm for arrival at Schiphol around midnight, he said. They then left for Israel at 3 am.
As a result of the forthcoming ban, it may be necessary to move the freighter operation, he said, and the Belgian airport of Liege would be the preferred option if the situation did not change.
However, he stressed, that nothing was yet definite.
Moving to Liege could also cause a problem for customers as consignments of flowers would have to be trucked from Liege to Amsterdam's Aalsmeer flower auctions, he said.
Ironically, he added, El Al had in the last few weeks been negotiating with Schiphol's cargo manager Frits Bisschop concerning a voluntary programme for the reduction of flights.
The airline was just about to sign an agreement under which it would reduce flights by 50 percent because of the noise problem , he said.
"I arrived back yesterday (Thursday) from Tel Aviv and found out about this ban," Chervin added.
